newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson thwarts burglary at his home.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson thwarts burglary at his home.

text.p: A man was arrested outside O.J. Simpson's mansion after the former football star apparently thwarted a burglary attempt, police said on Wednesday.

A Los Angeles Police Department spokesman confirmed a report by E! Entertainment Television that a suspect was taken into custody outside the Brentwood mansion in the early hours of Saturday morning after being confronted by Simpson, who was the subject of two highly publicised trials over the murders of his ex-wife and her friend.

The spokesman said no further details were immediately available, but E! said it had obtained a police report on the incident showing that at about 2:20 a.m. PDT (0920 GMT) Simpson confronted an intruder who had allegedly scaled the mansion's 8-foot (2.5 metre) wall and entered the residence through a back door.
According to E!, Simpson was awakened by the mansion's burglar alarm, found the back door unlocked and saw a man walking across the lawn toward the front door.

Quoting the police report, E! said Simpson asked the man "What are you doing, you set (off) the alarm." The man reportedly replied, "Yeah, everything just went off ... looking for Kato's residence." Actor Kato Kaelin was a houseguest of Simpson's at the time of the murders.

Simpson then ordered the man off the premises and electronically opened the front gate for him to leave. A private security officer, responding to the alarm, reportedly detained the intruder and held him until police arrived.
E! said the suspect, who was not named, was arrested and charged with attempted burglary.

Simpson no longer owns the mansion. It was auctioned off last week after a bank foreclosed on it because he had failed to keep up his montly mortgage payments. The house was bought for $2.6 million by Hawthorne Savings, the bank that foreclosed.

Simpson was aquitted of the July 12, 1994, murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman by a criminal court jury in October 1995, but was found liable for their deaths and ordered to pay the families of the victims $32.5 million by a civil court jury earlier this year.
